implementation_notes: kotlinx.coroutines implements the pattern's two halves almost literally: a MutableStateFlow<State> is a hot flow that always has a value, replays one latest value to new subscribers and conflates by equality (the exact contract of 'current state plus state stream'), while events arrive on a MutableSharedFlow<Event> or Channel<Event> processed by a coroutine collector, which keeps state updates sequential by default. Android's UI-state guidance uses this pair as the output API, collected with repeatOnLifecycle or collectAsStateWithLifecycle so production stops with the lifecycle; the ViewModel is the Bloc, and the reduced Cubit form is simply public methods calling update {}.
pitfalls: StateFlow conflates by equality: emitting a state equal to the current one is dropped, so states must be data classes with correct equals/hashCode or the update is invisible.
StateFlow never completes and cannot be closed: collection must be scoped (viewModelScope, repeatOnLifecycle) or the collector keeps running against a destroyed screen.
Exposing MutableStateFlow publicly lets any caller write state; expose asStateFlow() and keep the mutable instance private.
Collectors run on their collector context: heavy work in the reducer belongs on Dispatchers.Default (or a stateIn pipeline), not on the main thread.

variants.name: RxJava 3 subjects (pre-coroutines codebases)
variants.implementation_notes: Before kotlinx.coroutines became the norm, Kotlin UI code used the RxJava shape: BehaviorSubject<State> replays the latest state to new subscribers and a serialized PublishSubject carries events into a scan reducer, with toSerialized() required because the ReactiveX documentation states a subject's observer side is not thread-safe. It survives in large Android codebases and interoperates with coroutines through kotlinx-coroutines-rx3 (asFlow, awaitSingle), so a migration can expose Flow at the edges while internals stay Rx.
pitfalls: Mixing Flow and Rx in one feature gives two subscription lifecycles; bridge at a single boundary (asFlow) instead of observing both.
BehaviorSubject as a live holder leaks the Activity or View unless subscriptions are disposed with the lifecycle (CompositeDisposable in onCleared).
RxJava scheduler defaults surprise: state must be observed on the main thread for UI updates, while scan's reduction should stay pure and free of I/O.
throttle/debounce are the Rx half of event transformers, but they silently drop events - document which event types are allowed to be lossy.
